Mr. Chairman, I should like at the outset to apologize to the minister for something I said the other day when I spoke initially about the question of shipping and safety factors involved in shipping. I levelled the accusation that there had been a conspiracy of inaction and a conspiracy to do nothing. I want to withdraw that comment and to express my thanks to the Montreal

February 17, 1966
Supply-Transport
Star for having brought to my attention that I was in error.
Perhaps I could indicate what the Montreal Star had to say in an editorial on Tuesday, February 15:
The government has been accused of being a party to a "conspiracy of inaction" on matters relating to the safety of navigation in the St. Lawrence system. That, we suggest, is not quite right. A conspiracy is hardly possible without study, thought and planning. And the government can hardly be accused of any of these things -and more's the pity.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I should like to withdraw the reference to a conspiracy of inaction.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would mind sending me over that editorial.
In anticipation I had two photo copies made, so I will send the minister one.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: You might as well put it on Hansard and let us all see it.

Indeed, I think it is more a question of a pretty deliberate and intense indifference that is involved. I should like to make some comments about the answer the minister gave in the house on February 11 in a short reply to my initial remarks. Before I do that I should like to thank the minister for having sent me over, along with a covering letter signed in his own hand, an application for employment in the government service of Canada. I looked quite carefully at this application for employment, because the minister and I had jocularly made some comments about what value I might be to him.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I was stumped by the first question, which is "Position applied for". I quickly came to the conclusion that the only position vacant appeared to be that of the minister, and I must say I am not applying for it. I am not going to bother filling out the application.
I should like to make one or two references to Hansard for February 11, page 1118, where the minister is reported as saying:
He left the impression, I think, that because there were no regulations made under section 407 of the Canada Shipping Act, nothing had been done by the government or my department to insure the safety of the crews of ships. I
I am glad the minister admitted that no regulations had been made under or pursuant to section 407 of the Canada Shipping Act, because that is the section which refers to ships being manned by crews sufficient and

efficient from the point of view of safety of life. For the minister to have admitted that no regulations existed under that section is gratifying, at least for the admission itself.
The minister went on to point out, as he was quite able to do, that section 464 of the same act calls for a customs officer to detain a ship on the complaint of any person if he has reason to believe it is unsafe by reason of undermanning. The section provides that a steamship inspector rule on the question of no regulations existed under that section is cleared.
This is a correct interpretation of what section 464 says. What the minister failed to tell the house is that section 464 and the following section which also deals with the activities of customs officers and inspectors, as well as section 410 of the Canada Shipping Act had their origin in the merchant shipping act of Great Britain. All these sections were based on the United Kingdom practice, and when the Canada Shipping Act was initially passed we merely extracted these provisions from the British shipping act and put them into our law here. Under the British shipping act, and in every other shipping nation in the world, there are regulations which spell out the level of manning, but under section 410 of the Canada Shipping Act there is not a solitary word or regulation by the Governor in Council or even a letter from the minister that indicates what is the correct level of manning for ships.
Then the minister has the unmitigated gall to stand up in parliament and say that any sailor can complain to a customs officer if a ship is undermanned. He can do this under section 464. Of course he can. However, there is nothing in writing in any regulation or in statute form anywhere to indicate what is an undermanned ship, what is the correct level of manning. In addition to that, under section 466 of the Canada Shipping Act, if an individual does complain about the seaworthiness or the manning level of any particular ship, then the customs officer-let me read the section to you:
-he may exact from the complainant a deposit of money to defray the expanses of inspection and to pay any loss which may be sustained by the owner on account of the detention of the ship, or he may exact such security for the payment of such expenses or loss as he deems sufficient.
This provision is to guard against trivial or vexatious complaints, and those words are contained in the section. I ask the minister, how in heaven's name are you going to find the average sailor with anywhere upwards of $1,000 in his pocket to put up as security to a
February 17, 1966

customs officer if he lodges a complaint that the ship is undermanned? It is just arrant nonsense on the part of the minister, and he knows it-and he knew it when he made the statement-to make this suggestion. He made the statement, too, in the face of 40 people having been killed in shipping accidents last year and millions upon millions of dollars of damage.
Then the minister said there was a specific provision in section 164 requiring qualified mates and masters, and that these are constantly checked. In the first place the minister cited the wrong section, but that is understandable. In the second place, what is the value of placing reliance for safety measures entirely on the shoulders of masters and mates of ships when there is no requirement for efficiency levels or proficiency levels of the crew? Can the minister tell me what are the requirements for a wheelsman on the great lakes, the St. Lawrence seaway or the St. Lawrence river? Can he tell me what are the requirements for a boatswain or ordinary seaman so far as safety measures are concerned?
The minister shakes his head. He cannot because there are not any. Not more than 3 per cent of the Canadian sailors sailing on Canadian ships are certificated, and I am referring to the ordinary crews. Apart from the fact that the minister got the wrong section in his reference, he also drew the wrong conclusion, as if to leave the impression that there were some safety standard being imposed by himself or by his government.
Perhaps the minister unconsciously knew what he was talking about when he mentioned section 164, because it is an appropriate section to mention in passing. This is the section that allows shipowners to employ children on boats with wages in the range of $50 per month. Section 164 is the one that deals with the apprenticeship of any boy to sea service, and that it shall be by indenture between the apprentice and the master or owner of the ship requiring the apprentice. This provision relates to the old scheme which allowed shipowners to employ people at extremely low wages. Perhaps the minister unconsciously knew about it and was really trying to apologize for it when he referred to section 164.
Let us get back to the main point with which we should be dealing. My hon. friend from Timiskaming wants to know why the
Supply-Transport
minister has not got his advisers in front of him so they can advise him. He does not need them. He would not listen to them anyway. He has not so far, and I do not see the necessity for them. The other night the minister made a fantastic speech for about 25 minutes or so on the subject of a national transportation policy, and he wound up by saying that we did not have one.
In that fantastic speech he indicated that there was going to be a sort of vivisection take place within his department at the ministerial level. He was going to have a minister who would do the thinking, and that obviously excludes the current one. He was going to have a minister who would do the doing, and that excludes him. The only other portion of the sort of troika ministerialship over the Department of Transport for the present minister is the minister who does the talking.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
All we have had so far is talk. We have been given no reasons for this state of affairs or any indication of serious concern about the welfare and the lives of the people who sail the ships of this nation. We want specific answers. The people of Canada and the people who sail these ships also want specific answers. They want to know about the traffic control system.
Last November the promise was made that the question of a traffic control system would be studied. The minister told us that on the seaway we have the most advanced and finest traffic control system in the world. Incidentally, there is not the same need for a traffic control system at the locks because a ship cannot very well fall over there anyway. The minister said he had this fantastically efficient traffic control system on one part of the seaway, but while it was promised last November that a control system would be put into effect in the lower part of the seaway comprising the St. Lawrence River and gulf region not a word has been said about that.
Another question the sailors would like answered and which should be answered in this house is: What about the requirement for radiotelephone communication between ships to enable one ship to communicate with another and give an indication of the position of the one with respect to the other, what the weather is and what the situation is regarding visibility? In this regard the sailors were told last November by the minister's deputy that

February 17, 1966
Supply-Transport
the department was already drafting regulations with respect to the use of radiotelephones for this purpose. What about that matter?
There is also the question of a two way channel. The minister is arranging to build a second channel at the Welland locks, presumably one for upstream and one for downstream traffic. What about the lower part of the St. Lawrence seaway? This was another of the items upon which there was agreement between the Seafarers International Union, the underwriters and the ship owners. They agreed on the necessity of providing a two way channel. There was also agreement on the question of radio telephone communication and the necessity for a traffic control system.
We must be told clearly and concisely what is happening in the department with regard to these matters and what the minister is doing about them. There is also the overriding and important question of drafting and promulgating regulations under section 410 (1) (n) concerning the level of manning of ships so that people can see what is the legal minimum requirement for numbers and classifications of crew personnel on ships.
All of these measures, are designed for one purpose, to save the lives of people who man the ships that sail in and out of the ports of Montreal, Quebec and those on the Great Lakes. Maybe my words are harsh. Perhaps the minister has felt a little uncomfortable. Perhaps I have said things in an angry tone of voice. But just think, Mr. Minister, of the feelings of the widows of men who have lost their lives on that blessed seaway partly because of your failure to act, partly because we have a Canada Shipping Act that is older almost than these halls of parliament and contains provisions that are out of date. We have provisions that give the Governor General in Council authority to do things and they have not done them. Answers are required, action is required, but we need action more than answers.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot take very much more action at the moment than to give the committee the statement which I indicated I had with me the other day but which I had no time to give. In view of what the hon. gentleman has said this afternoon I think I have no choice now but to give the statement, though it is somewhat lengthy.

Before I do so may I say I am grateful to the hon. gentleman for giving me this editorial from the Montreal Star, because I inadvertently left my copy in my office. I want to point out that the editorial is completely and totally inaccurate in one of its statements when it says that I blandly-I do not know that I have ever done anything blandly but I am not making a point of that-assured parliament that traffic control on most parts of the seaway is as complete as it is anywhere in the world.
That is right.

The hon. member for
Skeena did not make a distinction in his speech the other day, though I tried to get him to do so, between the seaway and the St. Lawrence ship channel, which are two entirely different things. One is above Montreal and the other is below Montreal. I never said at any time that I was satisfied with the control on the St. Lawrence ship channel.
I never said you did.
Yes, you did.
I did not.
Well, we will not argue about it like two small children.
Just arguing like one small child is enough.

I am not satisfied and neither is anyone in my department with the conditions on the St. Lawrence ship channel, and I have never said I was. But if the hon. gentleman looks back to his speech he will see that he kept referring to the seaway, not to the ship channel. There were almost no accidents on the seaway last year because on the seaway there is a good and efficient control system. There were a regrettably large number of accidents in the ship channel and even in one or two cases in the port of Montreal itself, and a lot remains to be done before we can be satisfied with the provisions for safety.
As the hon. member pointed out, the government has received representations from a number of sources. He also referred to the meeting held in Montreal. Long before that meeting was held and ever since the department has been giving attention to every aspect of marine safety, and with the unfortunate sequence of serious collisions in the St. Lawrence River last year particluar attention has been paid to this area.
February 17. 196$

Various suggestions have been made for improvements in the law and in our procedures and facilities. All of these have received and will continue to receive not merely attention but wherever it is possible to take immediate action which seems to be justified that action will be taken.
I should like first of all to say a word about the separate ship channel system which is advocated by many of the users. One proposal that is frequently made is that in the interests of safety there should be duplicate channels in the St. Lawrence, one for up-bound and another for downbound traffic.
The problem in this connection is, first, to determine by hydraulic studies whether the project is capable of achievement without materially disturbing the level of the river and, second, its cost. Both of these processes have been going on. A scale model of the whole river channel is being built so that we can make sure that these very costly works, if they are undertaken, will accomplish what we want and not make the situation worse instead of better.
Studies in this field are being pursued, and so far as we can judge the cost would probably be as much as $225 million. Until we are quite sure of the effects on the water levels and on the strength and direction of the currents, this huge program cannot be embarked upon without the risk that the situation will be made worse rather than better.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
In 1967 the channel will be a minimum of 800 feet in width throughout its length except for a 20 mile stretch in Lake St. Peter where flow studies are being made prior to widening. By re-enforcing the requirement for up-bound and downbound ships each to keep to their own side we have a practical achievement of dual tracks in the existing system. However, it is apparent that additional and up to the minute information is required by the ships using the channel in order that collision with other ships may be avoided. I may say, answering the question raised by the hon. gentleman, that during the past 12 months the department has given intensive study to the traffic information and control system whereby a network of experimental shore-based v.h.f.-I believe that means very high frequency-radio stations has been established along the river from Montreal to Quebec. If our feasibility studies prove successful permanent equipment will be installed
Supply-Transport
and the system will be expanded to the limit of pilotage waters at Les Escoumins.
In the meantime ships which already are fitted with v.h.f. sets will be able to communicate with these existing stations during the next navigation season. Procedures are being developed to enable the latest information on traffic movements and weather conditions to be given to the ships in the system. Commencing with this traffic information service, the department expects to widen the scope of traffic surveillance and eventually to institute traffic control on a planned basis from Montreal to the open sea.
The next question has to do with the matter of radios on ships.
We have tried before and are renewing our efforts to encourage bridge to bridge communication between the large ships using the St. Lawrence system. Here we would take advantage of the fact that most of the foreign ships and all of our own lake ships using the river are fitted with v.h.f. radiotelephone sets. Until such time as the remaining ships are fitted the department has the ability to provide portable sets suitable for bridge to bridge communication, but not giving a full capability in ship to shore transmission in all parts of the river. We are working toward the introduction of a system of compulsory transmission of security calls at specified points as an additional aid to collision avoidance in the St. Lawrence.
The next question has to do with speed limits. Proposals which have been made to effect a general reduction of speed for vessels in these waters have been given careful consideration but, similar to other proposals for mandatory speed restriction to a fixed figure in conditions of limited visibility, the department feels that the extreme variety of ships and local conditions preclude formulation of such rigid rules, which, incidentally if they did exist, would be quite hard to enforce effectively. In a river such as the St. Lawrence the speed of each vessel is best governed individually through the advice of the local Canadian pilot to the ship's master. Although the relative speed of vessels in collision is a major factor in the seriousness of the resulting damage, a general reduction of speed for all ships in specified waters does not reduce the number of collision encounters requiring evasive action. The best aid to proper evasive action is preparedness for the encounter, which the department intends to provide by its traffic information service and

February 17, 1966
Supply-Transport
by promoting direct bridge to bridge communication between ships.
The next question has to do with manning and the scale of manning. It has been submitted, and the department has been seriously concerned with this aspect, that recent casualities have been caused by the lack of sufficient people aboard the ships. By regular inspections the officers of the department continue to enforce the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act requiring that every ship be sufficiently and efficiently manned. On the basis of studies made by the department the manning of ships is not held to be a contributing factor in the shipping casualties which have occurred in the St. Lawrence. Studies are continuing into the most effective employment of the men aboard ships and whether more formal requirements for watchkeeping duties should be laid down.
Because of the vast changes which are now being wrought in the shipping industry through the introduction of new and sophisticated methods of ship control, it would be inappropriate for the department to confirm manning standards which are based upon obsolescent concepts. What must now be done is to ensure that our studies keep pace with predictable trends in automation so that changes in manning can be anticipated and suitable provisions made.
The next question has to do with helmsmen. In respect of proposals which have been made to put Canadian helmsmen aboard foreign ships in pilotage waters, the department is satisfied that there have been no accidents attributable to a failure of communication between the pilot, the ship's officers and foreign crewmen at the ship's helm. It is preferable in narrow waters and here I am simply passing on the advice that has been given to me, to have a seaman who is thoroughly familiar with the handling characteristics of the ship rather than a local man put aboard a strange ship. Experience in steering is gained by the crew of a ship over a period of time in the open waters of the oceans before arrival in Canada and we cannot expect that a local man would require any less experience on each particular ship.
As to training, the training of Canadian seafarers is a matter about which the department has long been concerned, in the past by sponsoring nautical schools which the provincial governments now operate under the federal-provincial vocational training schemes.

Examination and certification of ships' officers and crewmen is conducted by the department and, based on the examination syllabi, guidance is given to the nautical schools in the matter of training programs.
We are waiting and still await, most impatiently I might say, because I have made some inquiries about this recently, the report of the Royal Commission on Pilotage, which was appointed by the previous government and which, I take it, must be doing a very thorough job, before turning attention to the problems inherent in the training and examination of pilots. In the wake of the vast changes in navigation techniques and current improvements in ship equipment, attendance at courses such as that for radar observer has been encouraged. This sort of training is especially necessary for those men who gained their qualifications before the general introduction of radar as a navigation and collision avoidance aid.
The department has under consideration a compulsory certification in radar observing for masters, mates and pilots, with periodic re-examination. But this, with the attendant increase in training facilities and administration, will be only a part of a long term project to keep certification standards for seafarers abreast of the times. For seamen there already exists the qualification as an A.B., able-bodied seaman, which some saltwater seamen have obtained. Work is progressing on a revision of the syllabus for this certificate so that men on our inland waters ships will be encouraged to improve their standing.
Qualification in marine emergency duties is another subject which the department has been anxious to see included in the syllabus of the nautical schools. This qualification would be open to all members of the crew. Extension of the training syllabus for life-boatmen is another matter now under review and a revision of this certificate of qualification may be made in company with the other innovations under study. These are the department's proposals which will certainly be brought forward by the minister as soon as it has been determined that the proposals made are sound.
We propose to put forward amendments to the Canada Shipping Act with a view to extending to foreign ships in Canadian waters the requirement for reporting wreck, collision and accident. At the present time this requirement includes only Canadian and
February 17, 1966

other Commonwealth ships. The department is rapidly training a number of officers, competent in the nautical field, to investigate marine casualties and accidents aboard ship in order to provide a much wider exercise of the powers conferred by the act in respect of the enforcement of safety regulations. Legal officers of the department will be assisted by specialized teams so that where warranted the department can move swiftly to learn the immediate causes of accidents and take corrective measures.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I think it will be seen from the outline I have given that the most serious attention has been paid to this problem. Its gravity is certainly underlined by the record of accidents and the loss of life in these accidents, which I regret as much as the hon. member does, during the last navigation season. It should not be forgotten in this context that the volume of shipping is rising at a rapid rate. The situation in this respect is not very different from the situation on the highways. When the volume of shipping in narrow waters increases the prospect of accidents does not only increase arithmetically but more than arithmetically; opportunities for collision are more than arithmetically greater, as hon. members know.
One of the great problems in enforcing traffic control on these waters is that it is not as easy to have speed cops as it is on the roads. Nearly all effective controls have to be directed from the shore. It is also true that the weather has been a contributing factor in the case of most of these accidents. Here again we are constantly seeking to improve the meteorological service and to make the benefits of forecasting available to shipping on a better basis than has been possible in the past. A great deal of progress has been made in this field. Nevertheless, as the hon. member for Saint John-Albert and I well know, the fog often comes down when the weatherman has not predicted it.

I do not
know what the minister is talking about when he talks of fog.

I can understand that,
coming from the hon. gentleman.
The one controversial question is whether the law or the regulations made under the law should lay down conditions for the overall manning of ships or whether the conditions laid down in this field should be selective. It has been the view of the department
Supply-Transport
up to now that selective regulations devoted exclusively to the safety of the ship are better than over-all regulations governing every man who is to be on the ship. I have been informed-I may be wrong about this-that in the United Kingdom there is not in fact detailed legal regulation of the manning of ships and that apart from those regulations which are required for the safety of ships manning is generally and largely a matter of collective bargaining. But we are continuing to look at this matter. I am informed by those who have studied it carefully that the investigations into the accidents which have taken place so far have produced little or no evidence that undermanning as such has been the cause. In those cases where causes could be clearly ascertained the accidents were nearly always the result of other factors.
It is true that radar has developed rapidly and has become more sophisticated. Unfortunately there are many ships' officers and even pilots who received their certificates some time ago and may not have advanced their training as rapidly as would be desirable in order to make the best possible use of these modern devices. I can assure the hon. member that we are taking every possible action in this field as fast as we can be sure that what we do is going to improve the situation.

I should like to make a passing comment, if I may. I am very happy that the department is considering all these things. Every statement which the minister made about every aspect of difficulty was to the effect that the matter was under study, was being examined, and that it had been under study for many years. Somewhere along the line it is necessary to get out of the study stage and do something.

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to be unfair. I told him we had in operation an experimental system along the shore between Montreal and Quebec using radios. We made radios available to those ships which did not already have them. I said they were required on all Canadian ships and that we were doing our best to have them installed on foreign ships using the channel where this could be done without undue interference with commerce. This is one of the points the hon. member raised. I also told him we were doing a practical study on the matter of two channels, and I do not think he would suggest we should consider letting contracts for something which might make the situation worse instead of better.

February 17, 1966
Supply-Transport

If the minister would not be so touchy and let me finish, perhaps we could deal with this question more rapidly. I say again I am happy that these matters are under study and consideration. What the minister told me was that the two items he mentioned were under study. He said that when he jumped up.
They are in operation. The hon. gentleman is almost deliberately misrepresenting me.

I can understand the sensitivity of the minister in this field where he is vulnerable. But perhaps, Mr. Chairman, you would have him contain himself for a moment. Let us consider what happens in the confined space of the St. Lawrence River or in the larger space of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Never mind the upper part which is probably correctly called the seaway. One ship travelling without radio communication facilities where there are other ships is like a car travelling without lights on a high speed highway at night. An experimental venture is not enough. If the minister is serious about the subject of radiotelephone communication between ships and a central traffic control system on shore, there must be compulsion and all ships must be required to use the radio communication system so that every ship may know where every other ship is. One ship without it is a liability.
That is quite true.

The minister says that is quite true. To my mind, what he is doing in these experiments is just another form of study, another way of examining this question. Why does he not take the steps which he knows must be taken and make this a mandatory requirement, if it is considered to be a worth-while safety measure, which it is in my opinion and that of everyone else who has gone into this question?
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The minister himself drew an analogy between travelling at sea and travelling on a highway. There is not any hesitation whatsoever by any provincial government or by any state of the union in the United States of America, if that is where proper jurisdiction lies, in saying that all cars travelling on highways at night must have their lights on, because they recognize it is a safety measure which is required in order to help preserve the lives of others. If the analogy is correct in

the one sense I submit it is correct in the other and that one blind ship travelling on the system is a hindrance to all other ships that may be travelling there.
A radio and television aid to navigation system is operated in New York harbour which involves u.h.f., the ultra-high frequency band. The area of water through which ships travel is scanned by groups of television cameras and information is transmitted to a particular type of receiver on the ships so that each ship can see at any precise moment what is happening around it in the area through which it is travelling.
Radar can be very misleading when it is relied on alone, because there is a blind spot in its coverage. This blind spot depends on the size of the ship and the height of the radar antenna. The blind spot covers a radius of many hundreds of feet for which area nothing is shown on the radarscope and in foggy weather or when visibility is low because of rain or mist this blind spot area is most crucial and dangerous. Knowing that a ship is proceeding some distance away is all right but not knowing what is within a 500, 600 or 700 foot radius is most disconcerting. Radar cannot show that but radio communication between ships can pinpoint other vessels in the area.
I think you are getting out of your depth, Frank.

I do not have the experience at sea which the hon. member had. All I did was to travel about on a small fish boat, but perhaps my hon. friend with his great experience may be able to enlighten the committee and bring his knowledge about these matters to bear on the minister, which could be worth while.
I am satisfied with the answers he has given.

The hon. member may be satisfied with the answers the minister has given but I have been in this chamber long enough to know that the very kindly and genial Minister of Transport never says anything plainly. I have come to expect that I must always take what he says with a grain of salt because I find that he always leaves something to be desired. He sets out on a course, as he did a while ago, of using a superfluity of words to cover up a paucity of information, and I must congratulate him on the success he achieves. But what we are concerned about is not words, we are concerned about the lives of the people who sail
February 17, 1966

the ships. I take the minister's word that he is concerned about them but I wish he would do something instead of just talking about the matter and explaining the studies and examinations which are being conducted in his department.
What we need is some action. Speeches are cheap. They do not cost anything to make, especially when somebody else writes them for you. Up to the present it has been the view of the government of Canada that icebreaking activities on the St. Lawrence River in wintertime should not extend to any attempt to keep navigation open between Quebec and Montreal. But there is a great deal of icebreaking activity, as the hon. member knows, that has to go on between Quebec and Montreal in order to prevent flooding, of which, in spite of our best efforts, we have had some regrettable examples this winter at the east end of the island of Montreal and along the shores of the St. Lawrence.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask another very definite question. giving a correct answer to that question. I will look into the situation right away and reply to the hon. gentleman.

What surprises me is that the minister should tell us that the cost would be prohibitive, when he does not even know how much it would be exactly. The Russians get through, and many other European ships built for navigation through ice are already at work. One or two extra icebreakers would be needed to keep the river open.
The minister said it would cost too much, but he does not know how much.
I wonder if the minister is not doing anything about it because he is afraid of offending some people. It is not a question of taking anything away from the Maritimes but of helping the port of Montreal and other ports between Quebec and Montreal, including the ports of Sorel and Three Rivers, by opening the St. Lawrence to winter navigation. Would the federal Department of Transport object to the provincial government using its own icebreakers? Has the minister anything to say about that?

So long as the government of the province of Quebec complied with the general laws of Canada in respect of navigation, which I am sure they would do if they had any ships, I know of nothing in the law which would prevent them from engaging in that kind of activity. I know of nothing in the law that would prevent any private company from doing so and, indeed, there are many private companies, as I am sure the hon. gentleman knows, which do own icebreakers or ships that are also icebreakers and are used in that way in their ordinary commerce. As a matter of fact, the department welcomes

service in the St. Lawrence River so that it year-round traffic is to be attained under any system of control, flood or otherwise, we will know what that cost is. Mr. Chairman, may I make a few representations on Vote 15 to the minister concerning railway service between the cities of Sherbrooke and Quebec. It is a service owned by the Quebec Central and the Canadian Pacific. I am looking at item 15 and I have some doubts whether this will be in order.

I think there was an understanding that the hon. member, having been good enough to allow the first item to go through last evening, could make his observations on one of the other votes. While it is true that this item does not directly relate to the particular railway I believe he has in mind, it does relate to railways and I hope the committee will give the hon. member its indulgence and allow him to make his observations on this vote.
Agreed.

There seems to be a fuss about the railway service between Sherbrooke and Quebec City. In fact there is only one train a day in either direction. The intention now, it appears, is to close down this service completely. Trains Nos. 1, 4 and 2 will be affected. So there is to be no passenger service at all between Quebec and Sherbrooke.
This affects close to three quarters of a million people living in the cities I have mentioned and in the various towns along the route, a distance of some 150 miles. Closing down this service, when one takes into consideration the other facilities existing in the region, is possibly the stupidest thing anyone could do. This is the only rail passenger service we have in the district between Sherbrooke and Quebec City.
The railway company claims it does not have sufficient passengers. Well, there is a damn good reason for that. Up to July 1, 1965, a one way ticket from Thetford Mines to Quebec City-Thetford is about half way between Sherbrooke and Quebec-cost $2.95. A return ticket cost $5.35. Now the fare is $3.85 one way and $7.70 return. This amounts to an increase of 90 cents on the one way journey and $2.35 on the return journey.
I do not have the cost of travelling directly from Quebec to Sherbrooke but I have the rate from Sherbrooke, to Thetford, the midway point. Up to July 1, 1965 it cost $2.75 one way and $4.95 return. The rates are now $3.60 one way and $7.20 return or $2.25 more on the return ticket. The railways say they cannot get enough passengers. That is not surprising. They used to offer a week end fare for students enabling them to travel between Quebec and Sherbrooke for $4.40 return. This rate has been abolished and the fare is $7.20 return. This is one good reason there are fewer passengers on that train.
Let me compare the rates charged by the C.N.R. on one train and by the C.P.R. on another. The C.N.R. rate from Sherbrooke to Montreal is $2.60. The other company charges $3.35 for the same journey. Furthermore there is only one connection, except on Sunday, which one can make to go to Montreal when travelling from Quebec via Sherbrooke to Montreal. It is necessary to stay over night in Sherbrooke and take the morning train to Montreal. That is the case except on Sunday night. I know this service. I have to use it to get here. I leave Thetford
February 17, 1966

Mines and get to Quebec City in the morning. It is only 300 miles but I arrive here at 9.30 at night because I have to cover more than 130 miles to catch a train in Quebec and then travel that mileage again along the north shore.
People do not take kindly to a policy ol this kind. They do not take the train unless they are obliged to do so. I think this company does everything in its power not to get passengers. In the first place they cannot provide a decent sandwich. The sandwiches are not edible. I wonder how anyone can chew them and still digest them. I think they pick them up somewhere after they have gone stale. There is no coffee service. Sometimes travellers can get a Pepsi but the supply often runs out during the trip. Remember, people have to sit on this train for four hours.
Yet this is what the pamphlet calls a fast dayliner. That is ironic. It is 150 miles between Quebec and Sherbrooke but it takes this train four hours. The speed works out to 37i miles an hour, slower than the first C.P.R. trains which steamed across Canada in 1885. Nevertheless there are representations from Sherbrooke, Quebec, Thetford and all the other towns along this line in favour of maintaining this service. It is the only one. It is still a necessity in this region. The company wants to close it down. It is doing everything in the book to prevent people using this service either by raising prices to a point at which people decide to take a bus or by other means. Compared with fares charged for comparable distances by the C.N.R. the C.P.R. rates are fantastic. People do not want to take the train when they are obliged to pay out such sums.
Yet on week ends the train is packed. Sometimes when I have taken it it has not been possible to find a place to sit down. I have seen people sitting on their suitcases. On week days passengers are few. If I did not have to take this train I certainly would not take it at such rates.
I believe the whole matter is now before the board. I should like the Minister of Transport to look into this matter and see whether there is not a possibility of lowering the fares charged and getting a better service on this train. At least let us have a decent sandwich or have the train stop at one station so that passengers can get a sandwich if they wish to do so. The journey takes four hours when the train is on time. I have known it to

be an hour and a half late. What is the average speed then? I leave the minister to figure that out. It is not much better than it was in the horse and buggy days. This is the Quebec Central Line. I believe the company is presenting arguments to the board in favour of abandoning the service because they have no passengers using the trains. I wish to draw the attention of the Minister to three points: the matter of security, the new plan for integration and the employees' protection.
With regard to security, the minister is undoubtedly aware of the situation, since I wrote him and since it is only a matter of changing locomotives during the two or three winter months. The letter I wrote the then minister of transport was returned to the board and, after that, I had to deal with fifteen offices before reaching the parties concerned. I was driven from pillar to post and ended up with the assistant superintendent and the superintendent. I was referred to Mr. Brunet about that matter and here is what I told him: I do not know if you are aware of this but I noticed a serious danger for the engineer and all the passengers.
Locomotive No. 3883 now being used is not suitable at all in the winter because of weather conditions. As a matter of fact, because of the snow, the engineer cannot see a thing for two or three miles. If there was an accident, the engineer would not even know about it, precisely because the snow covers the windows completely and the engineer is going ahead blindly.
Just think if an accident should happen in these circumstances? The engineer might be held responsible, but I assure you that I would be there, evidence in hand, because I always get the evidence-and the best way is to find out on the spot what is going on-and I would blame the C.N.R.
I am sure that the minister was not aware of the danger to which the passengers themselves were exposed when taking such a train. I made the trip myself with the engineers and the visibility was nil for four or five miles, and the train was going through level crossings. If an accident had happened, do you sincerely believe that you could have sworn in court that they had done all they could to avoid the accident?
We only asked to replace the first model with locomotive models 9300 or 9400 which take freight to Chibougamau.

I think that the passengers deserve much more attention than the freight trains. Those trains are used to get the logs down to Chibougamau, and all we asked was that they be used for the protection of the public.

Locomotives of the type mentioned in your letter are used indifferently on our passenger or freight trains, from coast to coast-

-and in weather conditions which are sometimes very unfavourable, and every effort is made to guarantee the safety of those we have the pleasure to serve.

This proves that he does not know much about it either. That is what you get when you look for the responsible party.
Now, Mr. Chairman, let me say that I wrote to the minister in this connection and then, finally, to Mr. Poitevin. I do not want to read the whole letter, but I quoted an article

entitled "C.N.R. to centralize Lake services". They are not doing it only in Roberval county, because Lake St. John and Lapointe counties are next in line.

I thank you. Although I am the manager of this particular sector, it seems, on the face of it, that you know more about alleged changes to be made in our service . . . than I do".

What will result from this, while we strive here to create employment? Eleven station employees will be laid off, more particularly the C.N.R. deliverymen who have been providing us with excellent service for 30 years at no cost to the railway. All those employees will no longer be serving the population. Mr. Chairman, after the express car is removed, the passenger service will simply be discontinued.
That is what they are aiming at they want to get a bus to transport us throughout the riding, by bus, by car, by anything.

Those improvements were appreciated by the public as evidenced by our revenues.

Let me however, bring a slight correction concerning the unfavourable remarks you formulated on the "service" item at the C.N.

There is talk of a 28 per cent increase and taking off the express car and cancelling the passenger service next summer or perhaps next autumn. A service very much like that of the Quebec Central mentioned earlier by the

member for Megantic; we cannot go above 35 or 40 miles per hour on our line.

Three small Quebec inspectors came because down our way they do not come one by one, they come three at once, not just one inspector, a man alone but three inspectors from Quebec or Montreal to close the lunch counter.

Everything was done to discourage the employees. There was the famous manager's commission on the express, which encouraged him to open the station, even on Sunday. Mr. Chairman, I should like to put one question only concerning item 20 with regard to construction of buildings, terminal facilities, etc.
The minister is aware that we have in Rouyn-Noranda three railway stations: an O.N.R. station in Rouyn-Noranda, an O.N.R. station in Noranda, and a Canadian National station in Noranda. Is the department considering a project to set up a union station which might be called "Rouyn-Noranda"? There would be one station only to serve the people over there. This station would eliminate grade crossings in Rouyn and in Noranda.
I shall be glad to look into that question right away.

Item agreed to.
25b. Payments in respect of Maritime Freight Rates Act and for supplemental pension allowances to railway employees-To extend the purposes of Transport Vote 25 of the Main Estimates for 1965-66 to include payments to provinces as contributions, as detailed in the estimates, to assist highway construction related to the abandonment of railway branch lines, $1,250,000.

This vote relates to the construction or rebuilding of the Moncton-Buctouche highway which is related to the abandonment of the Canadian National Buctouche branch line. I should like to know, first of all, if special circumstances obtained which enabled the government to make this particular grant toward the building of a highway to take the place of the railway. Second, is it general policy and will this policy be applied to other abandonments? These are rather general questions but I hope the minister has some answers.

I wonder if I could give a very brief answer now and then undertake to discuss the matter at greater length on my estimates for the coming year or at any other time? The brief answer is that this particular
Supply-Transport
branch line was losing a lot of money annually but it was serving a community. It seemed to the government that rather than throw away a lot of money in annual losses, if we could capitalize the losses and allow part of the saving for the building of the road and take part of the saving for the treasury, everybody would be better off. I should like to elaborate a bit on that on another occasion because I think the principle can be applied elsewhere and I am happy to say my colleagues agree with me.

Item agreed to.
Air Services-.
30. Administration, operation and maintenance including the administration of the Aeronautics Act and regulations issued thereunder, the administration of the Radio Act and regulations issued thereunder, Canada's share of the costs of the international radio, telegraph and telephone organizations listed in the details of the estimates, Canada's assessment for membership in the World Meteorological Organization, $110,000 for grants in aid of meteorological research in Canadian universities and Canada's share of the cost of the World meteorological Organization symposium on design of hydrometeorological networks, $97,637,700.

I should like to draw the attention of the minister to a matter pertaining to a class of employees in his department known as radio operators. Perhaps the minister, or his deputy who is advising him, is familiar with this category so I will not need to go into too much detail. Briefly, the situation is that in 1962-63 the Civil Service Association of Canada submitted to the Department of Transport and the Civil Service Commission reasons for a better and more realistic career program for radio operators.
The minister will be glad to know that the fault from this point on does not lie with his department. Following the normal procedure the Department of Transport submitted their recommendation to the Civil Service Commission, but unfortunately the Commission did not agree. Nothing has been done for this particular class of employee since that time, as I understand it. The end result, Mr. Chairman, has been that the department has experienced an acute shortage of this type of employee.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Because of inadequate wages and lack of opportunity for promotion and advancement too many radio operators, I understand, are leaving the department and it is difficult to recruit and train people in this particular category. Promotions have been held back

February 17. 1966
Supply-Transport
because of the shortage, and even the vacation schedules have been cancelled. As I understand it, the morale of this group is very low.
The total salary paid this class of employee reaches a peak of $408 a month, which seems to me to be too low at this particular time. The recommendation that these people have made to me as their representative, and I am sure it has been made to others, is that the minister should look at the matter and see whether something can be done for this particular type of employee. I have every confidence that the minister will do so at the earliest opportunity.
This is one speech I am really grateful for, Mr. Chairman, and I think it is going to help the minister.

I should like to draw the attention of the minister to a situation at Winnipeg airport. I think the minister arrives at Winnipeg often enough to know that when you deplane from an arriving aircraft you have to proceed to the second floor by staircase. This makes things particularly difficult for older people. If you are arriving at the airport to catch a plane you can take an escalator up but when you arrive at Winnipeg you have to walk up the stairs carrying bags and so forth.
I hope the minister will take a look at this and see whether it is possible to instal escalators for the use of people arriving at the airport. Naturally this is one of the airports I use quite often and I have noticed on several occasions elderly people particularly, who perhaps have heart conditions or other ailments, having to climb these steep stairs to get to the second floor so that they can get down to the ground level on the other side. This seems a ridiculous sort of situation. I hope the minister will give careful consideration to the installation of at least one escalator which can be used by people who are not supposed to climb stairs.

Mr. Chairman, I might say that this would repair in part the damage the
February 17, 1966

minister has done to Winnipeg by his faulty commitment with regard to the Winnipeg-Chicago route and he might even make one or two friends.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to know if it is section 30 which deals with broadcasting. This concerns necessarily section 30, and if the minister is agreeable, I am going to discuss it at once.

I want to speak on the subject of radio broadcasting, Mr. Chairman, and I was just asking the minister whether that subject would come under item 30.

Not unless the hon. gentleman wants to speak only about the technical side of licensing. If it is any other aspect of broadcasting he should speak on the estimates of the Secretary of State, not on mine.
Licensing is under the minister's jurisdiction.

It depends on the particular aspect of licensing. On licensing in general the B.B.G. reports to the Secretary of State, so I would think that what the hon. member wants to bring up would be more appropriate to that department.

It will not take me very long to deal with this matter. If the minister judges that it is a matter for the Secretary of State to answer I will leave it at that and bring up the problem again before the Secretary of State. What I have in mind is this peculiar situation which exists in regard to small, local radio broadcasting stations. They have a permit to operate during the daytime on, say, 1,000 watts but at sundown they reduce their power to a lower wattage.

If the hon. gentleman will permit me, I think that is definitely a matter which would be within the purview of the Board of Broadcast Governors. If the hon. gentleman would agree, I think it would be preferable to bring that matter up when the hon. lady's estimates are before the committee.

I will do that.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)

I have a few observations to make to the minister. May I first ask him if the department has made any progress toward setting up an examination board under
Supply-Transport
the Aeronautics Act, similar to that set up in the United States whereby a pilot who has suffered some physical ailment and has recovered has to undergo a doctor's examination and be O.K.'d by him. That has to be done before he receives his pilot's licence again. Second, may I ask a question having to do with community antenna television. I do not know whether to address it to the minister at this time but I should like to know what steps he proposes to take and whether this will be placed under the control of the Board of Broadcast Governors.

The answer to the first question is yes. Steps have been taken and I understand that the appropriate body should meet tomorrow. The answer to the second question, if the hon. gentleman would grant us his indulgence, is that I do not think that the situation is going to be changed, but he will have an opportunity to inquire into it under my next set of estimates.

I should like to seek from the minister some suggestions or advice. I am not sure whether he can be of direct assistance in this matter. If he cannot assist us, then I hope that he or the members of his department can direct me to the appropriate channels. My inquiry has to do with weather reports and weather broadcasting. In our area we receive weather reports from the airports at London and Windsor. Under the direction of the local Federation of Agriculture and of Mr. Harold Smith of the radio station, who is also farm editor, a drive has been inaugurated because of the intensive farming in that area to have much more complete and comprehensive weather coverage. Because of that farming we need comprehensive weather coverage. My purpose in interceding on this particular vote is to request from the minister information as to what approaches may be made to have weather broadcasts with respect to the particular areas involved and as to what facilities may be sought along this line. The minister need not answer me now. If he wishes to take note of what I have said and let me know at an appropriate time it will be appreciated.
I should like to write to the hon. gentleman, if I may, after I have made inquiries.

May I put to the minister a question relating to the construction and hard surfacing of airport runways at the Winnipeg satellite airport of St. Andrew's. I should like to ask the minister if that question would

February 17, 1966
Supply-Transport
arise under this item or would he prefer that I put the question under another item?
It should be, I believe, under the next item.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask one short question of the minister. I am not sure whether this is the appropriate vote on which to ask the minister this question but I am concerned with the problem of the definition of an air-cushion vehicle. It is my understanding that in recent weeks a decision has been given by, I am told, the Department of Justice with regard to air-cushion vehicles which are known to the general public as hovercraft.
The Department of Justice has designated it as an aircraft. The definition poses some difficulties because this vessel, if one may call it a vessel, is completely new in conception. It is a completely new form of transportation. It is neither ship nor aircraft but something in between which requires a solid surface two or three feet beneath it in order to operate. I am given to understand that by categorizing this craft as an aircraft considerable difficulties will be caused in the development of this particular type of machinery, if I may call it that, or this particular method of transportation which could have very great benefits for our country.
I am wondering if the minister is planning to take up this matter with the Department of Justice? I think that this type of vessel could be better designated by the Deparment of Transport marine services if it were classified as a hover craft or an air-cushion vehicle with characteristics more akin to those of a ship than those of an aircraft.
We are discussing this matter with the Department of Justice but I am afraid that we have not reached any conclusion yet.

Mr. Chairman, I notice under an item in vote 30 mention of the operation and maintenance of airports and other ground services. We have an airport in the constituency I have the honour to represent, the constituency of Saskatoon, and it is a large airport with a jet runway. For several years now we have been assured that, since we have the runway and the facilities, and certainly we have the passengers, jet aircraft would be stopping at our city. However, I was disappointed to notice in Hansard yesterday, as I mentioned in my question today, that the short range DC-9 jet aircraft are not
[Mr. Schreyer.i
going to be stopping in the province of Saskatchewan. I should like from the minister some assurance-
I am sure that the hon. member will have noticed that that only applies to the period up to July 1.

I believe, sir, that if I read the announcement correctly it was to the effect that this would be so for this year but that it might be changed in subsequent years when further aircraft become available. It did not say up to July 1 as I read it in Hansard of yesterday.
I should like some assurance, sir, that efforts will be made very soon indeed to see that DC-9 service is provided to our province and to our city because we are becoming more industrialized. Mineral developments are certainly beginning to expand, and in that regard I refer to potash. We have tremendous numbers of people coming into the province. We do not have the facilities there that we think we should have. I think it is essential, since we have been promised a short range jet service for three years, to have that service. Frankly, sir, I should like your assurance that as soon as possible you will see that we in Saskatchewan will no longer be a have-not province. I assure you, sir, that we are not the poor country cousins we were a few years ago.
May I call it six o'clock?
I will give that representation the most "liberal" consideration that I can, sir.
Thank you, sir.
