speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
It is my duty in conformity with standing order 39A, to inform the house that the following questions will be discussed on the adjournment motion tonight: The hon. member for Okanagan-
February 17, 1966

Revelstoke (Mr. Johnston), Immigration -reported increase in applications from Rumania; the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman), Post Office Department-steps to overcome loss on second class mail; the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette), municipal development loan fund-inquiry as to extension of period.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
It being six o'clock the house will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely, notices of motion for papers, private bills and public bills.

The house resumed from Thursday, February 3 consideration of the motion of Mr. Bell (Carleton):
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all reports, briefs or other documents of communications received by the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor-General or the Department of Justice from the Law Society of Upper Canada relating to Mr. Justice Leo Landreville; all replies made to any such reports, briefs or other documents or communications; all letters or other communications addressed by the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor-General or any officer of the Department of Justice, since the 1st day of January 1964 to Mr. Justice Leo Landreville; all replies made by Mr. Justice Leo Landreville or by any solicitor or agent on his behalf to any such letters or other communications.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the motion of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) I should like to preface my remarks by stating that I am a little anxious as to how to proceed. I notice that those who have opposed the motion of the hon. member for Carleton have used a ploy commonly adopted by those who have a weak case. They have referred to matters outside the scope of the question.
I have in my hand the debates of the House of Commons for February 3. I notice that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) referred to the fact that the hon. member for Carleton speaks loudly and fast. I hope I am not speaking too loudly or too fast for members of the house. Then the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme), supporting the Minister of Justice, said he did not like the tone of voice used by the hon. member for Carleton. Again, on page 675, we find the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) objecting to the belligerency of the hon. member for Carleton. Mr. Speaker, if I go too fast or speak too loudly or appear
Motion for Papers
too belligerent, or if members do not like the tone of my voice, please let me know and I will try to accommodate myself so as to meet the wishes of those who would otherwise raise objections so as to try to deny to other members of the House of Commons the privileges which are their right.
I have strong feelings on this question of the cabinet laying this message from the benchers of the Law Society of Upper Canada on the table. I have been elected to this house on three occasions. On the first and second occasions of entering parliament I was not sworn in until the day parliament opened. But on the third occasion, after the election of November, 1965, I made a special trip to Ottawa early in December because I felt then, as I feel now, that the cabinet is making a mistake in refusing to table for the benefit of members of the House of Commons a letter they have received from the benchers of the Upper Canada Law Society. I was sworn in by the Clerk of the House on December 6 and the moment I had signed the roll I asked him how I could make a motion for the production of this paper from the benchers of the law society. He directed me to another official. I went to his office and prepared the necessary papers. That was in December.
I should like to advise hon. members that when I came to the house on January 18 I found that my motion for the production of the benchers' missive had not been placed in Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day. I immediately went to an official of this house and asked him what had happened with regard to my action of December 6. It was explained to me that there was some thought of withholding my request because if a foreign government writes to this government and expresses some opinions such missives are not tabled in the house without the consent of the foreign government concerned being received in advance.
Comparing the benchers of the Upper Canada Law Society with a foreign government may well be flattering to the benchers, but I stated that in my view they were nothing but a private group of lawyers who had no public authority, and I did not see any reason why my request was being delayed. If hon. members will look in Votes and Proceedings they will find it listed under the date January 19, though I filed it on December 6.
On February 3 the hon. member for Carleton speaking to his motion, one to which I give wholehearted support, went out of his

February 17, 1966
Motion for Papers
way to make a remark with which I cannot agree. I wish to correct the impression he may have created. The hon. member made this comment:
I want to point out that even in respect oi this motion the Minister of Justice could not refrain from playing politics. The hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) had a notice of motion on the order paper dealing with this subject and covering the first part of my motion. It was listed as No. 21 and therefore was on the order paper preceding mine, which is No. 39. But yesterday there was arranged the standing of the motion of the hon. member for York-Humber who is a supporter . . . of the minister's party, in order to deal with this later motion by an opposition member. Is there anybody anywhere in this chamber who has any doubt of the reasons for this?
I was amazed to hear the hon. member make that statement because he must be the only member of the House of Commons who did not realize that on February 2 there were 1,600 Liberals in metropolitan Toronto attending a dinner given for the Prime Minister of Canada and Mrs. Pearson. I had made arrangements weeks in advance to have dinner with the Prime Minister's brother who sat at my table. I rode to Toronto on February 2 on the same train with the Prime Minister. Yet the hon. member for Carle ton asks: "Is there anybody anywhere in this chamber who has any doubt of the reasons for this?" He is referring to the standing of my motion. He must be the only member of the house who did not know that every Toronto Liberal member was out of the house on that day attending this dinner at the Royal York.
In rising to support the present motion I would add this statement: If the motion should be voted down, and I hope it will not be, in order to save a further black mark against the record of this cabinet, I will press ahead with my own motion because the members of this parliament are being denied the right of examining a document which has been forwarded to the cabinet as the executive arm of the government and we are getting into a position where members of the cabinet are telling each and every one of us: It is not good for you to see these things; you are not smart enough to comprehend the meaning of such a missive; leave it to those of us who are in the cabinet; we are the smart boys and we can give you the answers.
There has been a lot of fluff during this discussion about the independance of the judiciary being called into question. Speakers have said we were criticizing the actions of Mr. Justice Landreville. They have said we

are blackening the record of a man who has no means of defending himself.
On February 3 the Deputy Speaker-he is now in the Chair-had to make a ruling during the course of the discussion. He said: "The issue before the house is whether or not certain documents should be tabled." He repeated that statement. "The only issue before the house in this debate is whether or not the papers mentioned in the motion should be tabled."
I am in favour of the tabling of these papers. An interesting angle in connection with this discussion has been the assertion developed on the side that we have no right to discuss this matter because it has been referred to a commission-a commission consisting of Mr. Justice Rand, a retired judge from Moncton, New Brunswick. Now this problem arises: Cannot the highest court in the land discuss a matter which has been referred to a commission, a body which in the last resort is obviously junior to parliament as the highest court?
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
On October 15, 1957, the government of the day by order in council appointed a committee to inquire into the natural energy resources of this country. That was on October 15. On the 17th of October Mr. M. J. Cold-well, the then hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, rose in his place and, during the course of his remarks with regard to the affairs of the day, stated:
Naturally, I welcome the appointment of the royal commission to study the question of the use of Canadian energy resources and to ensure the most effective use of such resources in the public interest, but I am not unmindful of this, that the present party in power is faced with a problem in this regard because of its attitude in the house during the pipe line debate. I could not put my finger on it today but I know it is in Hansard where a former prime minister said that the establishment of a royal commission was often an excellent way of shelving a difficult problem. I hope that the setting up of this royal commission to deal with energy, oil, gas, pipe lines, and so on, is not being undertaken in order to shelve a very important problem. I think such a study is entirely desirable and, indeed, overdue.
However, there are a number of matters on which it is necessary that action should be taken before the report of any royal commission is available. Indeed, they are questions of policy that should not be shelved. I am thinking particularly of the reference of the matter of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited to the royal commission. I note that the question is referred in this way and I am quoting it:
"Whether in view of this special relationship to the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation and the nature of its financing and control any
February 17, 1966

special measures need to be undertaken in relation to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited in order to safeguard the interests of Canadian producers or consumers of gas."
Upon which Hon. Howard Green, who I presume was acting government house leader, rose up and objected to Mr. Coldwell making any comments on a matter that had been referred to a royal commission. Mr. Coldwell then stated that in his opinion he had every right to refer to a royal commission appointed two days previously because, after all, this was the highest court in the land.
It is quite interesting to note that the hon. Lionel Chevrier was sitting in oppposition in October, 1957, and he took part in the debate. He supported Mr. Coldwell and in answer to Mr. Green he said:
There is nothing sub judice. In the circumstances I submit to you, sir, with deference, that the hon. member has every right to do what he is doing.
That is, that the hon. member had every right to discuss the matter referred to a royal commission appointed two days previously.
The Speaker gave a ruling on the matter and the Speaker was Hon. Roland Mich-ener. He was a roommate of the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada at Oxford and I presume some of the brilliance of our leader rubbed off on him, because on October 17, 1957, as recorded at page 119 of Hansard, he stated:
I think I have heard enough to determine the matter. There is nothing on the order paper which would preclude a discussion of this matter. The royal commission is not a court of record and matters before it are not sub judice. Therefore I see no reason why the hon. member should not discuss it.
Then the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), who is supposed to know everything about the rules of this house, and who was leader for the official opposition, when I was in opposition, shouted across toward Mr. Green:
Closure by order in council.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that when we are told we cannot look at this missive from the Law Society of Upper Canada because the matter has been referred to a royal commission we are having closure by order in council in this day and age, in 1966.
I have here a copy of the order in council, dated January 19, 1966, appointing Mr. Justice Rand. My submission is that this letter could have been produced on January 18 if members of parliament had asked for it in the ordinary way. But on January 19, just as Mr. Coldwell stated in 1957, a royal commission was appointed and now we are given 23033-89
Motion for Papers
closure by order in council. I am simply quoting the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who knows a great deal more about parliamentary practice than I do, and I am willing to accept his leadership on the matter of the rules covering the conduct of the house.
This matter of whether or not we can ask for these papers before the decision of the royal commission comes down is enlightened by a report in the Toronto Daily Star of Tuesday, February 8. Mr. Jack Biddell, president of the Clarkson Company, had spoken at a meeting of the Empire Club in Toronto and made some uncomplementary remarks with regard to officials of the Atlantic Acceptance Corporation which collapsed in the biggest financial scandal in Ontario in many years.
The Ontario government has appointed a royal commission consisting of Mr. Justice Hughes to inquire into the Atlantic Acceptance debacle. The day after Mr. Biddell made his speech before the Empire Club in Toronto, in which he referred to "arrogant scoundrels"-incidentally, Mr. Speaker, did you ever hear that word "arrogant" used in any other place than before the Empire Club in Toronto-Mr. J. E. E'berle, lawyer for C. Powell Morgan, former president of Atlantic Acceptance, argued before Mr. Justice Hughes that Mr. Biddell should be cited and censured for his action since the matter was before the royal commission.
But Mr. Justice Hughes, a member of the Supreme Court of the Province of Ontario, a gentleman appointed to the bench by the government in Ottawa, said the royal commission was not conducting a trial but an inquiry. I point out that this commission of Mr. Rand is not conducting a trial. It is conducting an inquiry. The order in council specifies:
The committee of the Privy Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, advise that the Honourable Ivan Cleveland Rand, of Moncton, in the province of New Brunswick, be appointed a commissioner under Part 1 of the Inquiries Act to inquire into the dealings of the Honourable Mr. Justice Leo A. Landreville with Northern Ontario Natural Gas Limited or any of its officers, employees or representatives, or in the shares of the said company, and to advise whether, in the opinion of the commissioner, anything done by Mr. Justice Landreville in the course of such dealings constituted misbehaviour in his official capacity as a judge of the Supreme Court of Ontario, or whether the honourable Mr. Justice Landreville has by such dealings proved himself unfit for the proper exercise of his judicial duties.
That is the foreword to the appointment of that commission of inquiry. It is not a court

February 17, 1966
Motion for Papers
of trial. We are not trying Mr. Landreville here. We are not making any accusations. We are not making any innuendoes. As members of parliament we are asking the cabinet to lay on the table the communication received from the benchers of the Law Society of Upper Canada.
In the discussions that have taken place already the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has asked, "What have you got to say about the action of the law society keeping it a secret document?" The law society is a private body. They can do what they like with their own property, but when the law society writes to a public body like the House of Commons then the members of the house are entitled to see what the contents of that communication are.
One of the speakers in this debate, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey), in a direct reference to Mr. Justice Landreville used this phrase, "whom we must presume innocent." Nobody who has spoken in support of the motion moved by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has made any statement about the innocence or guilt of Mr. Justice Landreville. All we want is for the cabinet to table the letter received from the benchers of the Law Society of Upper Canada.
The hon. member for Verdun made several references in the course of his remarks to the doubt in his mind as to the action of the cabinet in withholding communications from members of the house. It is interesting when you find a man defending the actions of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin), but still expressing doubt as to what he is doing. I simply ask the members of this house to make certain that the cabinet produces this letter.
I admire the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) who the other day, quoted Professor Chapman's book, "British Government observed", in particular the following passage:
This passion tor secrecy has . . . psychological and sociological origins. Secrecy in public life panders to a craving for a sentiment of self-importance. of belonging to an inner circle.
I say that is the attitude that members of the cabinet are adopting on many questions. For instance, I asked how much money was paid to Mrs. Baskin, an employee of the civil service, wife of a former member of this house, and how much was paid to Mrs. Sauve. The government told me the amount of money they paid Mrs. Baskin but what Mrs. Sauve gets is entirely a secret matter.

How self-important and arrogant can members of the cabinet get? I say we are the highest court in the land and I ask for the production of these papers as requested by the hon. member for Carleton.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, having just heard the eloquent (Mr. Cowan), I am almost nervous about words of the hon. member for York-Humber becoming involved with those who are accused of having a passion for secrecy; yet I do believe that this motion ought to be turned down by this house. I must say that I do so with some trepidation for the reason that my colleague, the deputy leader of this party, has spoken in favour of the motion. 1 have always found him persuasive and frequently sound but I regret to say that on this motion I found him to be neither.
I am particularly interested in this matter because, like the deputy leader of this party, I am a member of the bar. I should say that my courage is bolstered by the fact that another learned colleague of mine, the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott), also spoke against the motion. I am particularly interested in this matter as a member of the bar in the province of Ontario. I think I can claim a special interest because I was the first member of this house to urge upon the previous minister of justice the necessity, in the interests both of the administration of justice and of fairness to Mr. Justice Landreville, whose conduct has been widely criticized in the press, that action be taken.
I am not claiming that it was because of my suggestion that the course of action taken was taken, but I did suggest to the minister that one of the proper preliminaries in dealing with this matter was an investigation by a person of high standing such as the present commissioner, Mr. Justice Rand. I should like to point out to members of this house that this matter is rather serious because, according to the information supplied to me by Dr. Eugene Forsey, whose studies of matters of this sort are well known to most of us-
That is a matter of opinion, as you suggested to me a moment ago.
I am not quoting Dr. Forsey as an expert on every conceivable subject.
Only in respect of those with which you agree.

That is right. On this particular occasion Dr. Forsey supplied me and perhaps other members of the house with a memorandum on the subject of the removal
February 17, 1966

of Superior Court judges. He pointed out that this was unique and that there has been no occasion in Canadian history when this matter has been dealt with, but there have been one or two abortive attempts to deal with this matter: On no occasion before has it reached the point the present case has reached. Let me remind members of this house that the only authority with power to remove a Supreme Court judge is the Governor General on an address of the Senate and House of Commons. Before the Senate and House of Commons deal with such a matter it is entirely appropriate that there be a preliminary inquiry.
By whom should a preliminary inquiry be carried out, Mr. Speaker? I suggest that the course chosen by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) is perfectly sound. He selected as a preliminary course an inquiry by an eminent retired justice of the Supreme Court of Canada who could not be accused in any sense of being biased or prejudiced in this matter in any shape or form. This inquiry is now to take place. What possible justification is there, in view of that fact, for this house to demand that some opinion expressed by, as the hon. member for York-Humber has said, a private body of lawyers be made a public document at this time? Why should their opinion, simply because it has been sent to the Minister of Justice in the nature of a complaint, as has been rumoured, by the majority of the benchers of the Law Society, and correspondence between the Minister of Justice, Mr. Justice Landreville and the Law Society, be made public?
Of course publicity is an important thing at certain times, but I suggest if we have a genuine respect for the independence of the judiciary we should not want to set a precedent as a result of which a complaint, at any time one is received by the minister of justice regarding the conduct of a judge, would as the property of this house be made a public document. I suggest this would not only interfere with the independence of the judiciary but would restrict the freedom of an individual to criticize the judiciary at the right times and in the right places. I believe that if I have a complaint about the conduct of a judge, and those of us who lose cases do sometimes feel disturbed about a judge's conduct, I should be permitted to voice that complaint in confidence. Sometimes there are serious complaints about judges. I am not suggesting for one moment that they occupy 23033-89J

a sacrosanct position but, if every time some disappointed or dissatisfied litigant writes to the minister of justice that correspondence may be made public, a dangerous situation would be created.
I agree with what the hon. member for York-Humber said about how arrogant cabinets formed from parties on both sides of this house and throughout the world are in using the excuse of secrecy to conceal documents. No doubt that will be improved when this party finds itself in that position over there but until that time we will always have the spectacle of arrogant cabinets. I agree with those arguments but they have no application to this case.
There are situations in which there is no public benefit served by the production of documents. We know, because Mr. Justice Rand has made this statement, that there is to be a public inquiry into this matter. That is why I found the argument of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) so completely non-persuasive. He said he was concerned about the independence of the judiciary and no doubt he is, but then he proceeded to say that in this case if we did not make the documents public immediately in this house, even though there is to be a public inquiry, the public would become suspicious and we must not feed their suspicions. It may be that we must not feed the suspicions of the public, but I think we would do so far more by making public the results of inconclusive and ex parte inquiries than by waiting for the results of the public inquiry that is to be made.
A proper inquiry has been instituted in accordance with perfectly proper and legitimate practice. Why do we need further documents and correspondence put before this house? We may have to deal at a later date with this matter in the form of a joint address but we do not know that at this stage. We may never have to deal with it. The commissioner may report that there is nothing to be dealt with and neither the government nor any other member needs bring it to the attention of this house. Until then what need have we for this correspondence and these documents? I do not care what the Law Society of Upper Canada says. The hon. member for York South suggested that this information should be made available because the Law Society has complained but he knows, as I do, that the Law Society is a completely oligarchic institution.

If the hon. member complains about the actions of the Law Society of Upper Canada, why does he not go to that Law Society and ask for the documents instead of supporting this motion in the house as a means of producing these documents? If the production of these documents would serve the administration of justice or would serve the cause of fairness in dealing with the serious problem that has been raised in regard to this particular judge, if I could see any use for it at all then I would support the motion. I can see no useful purpose but I can see a very dangerous precedent being set which would undermine, whether we like it or not, the independence of the judiciary. Whether the originator of the motion saw that danger or not I do not know, but I am sure he would disclaim that intent.
We are not just dealing with one case and one individual judge; we are dealing with a precedent that would affect the whole administration of justice. I submit to hon. members that the production of these documents would serve no useful purpose and would in fact establish a dangerous precedent. Mr. Speaker, this is a matter of some serious consequence. Following the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), I am not going to refer to the issue of the independence of the judiciary and whether or not the alleged misbehaviour of Mr. Justice Landrevillle took place before or after he was appointed because I do not think it is a matter of serious consequence. But it is a matter of some consequence that we are really arguing about the qualification of judges, or at least the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) is in putting forward the motion.
No, not at all.

I want the hon. member for Carleton to hear me out so that I may

impress upon him the seriousness of this type of motion. There is one point that is very important and it is this. There has been a report from the benchers of the Upper Canada Law Society. Who are these benchers? They are not sanctified in any way whatsoever. They do not come down to us from Mount Olympus with any sort of aura. They are the elected executive of a very tight trade union. They are elected by the members of the legal profession of Ontario to protect the legal profession to a great extent.
These benchers rule on whether or not members of the legal profession from other provinces may practise in Ontario. They have a heavy hand in deciding, for the good of the profession, how many graduates are going to leave Osgoode Hall. They have something to say about minimum fees and tariffs. In other words, they are no more or no less than the executive of the plumbers' association. The service station association has an executive, as has the medical profession and the legal profession. These benchers are the people who sent this letter. It is not a report from the Law Society because the Law Society is composed of all the lawyers in the province. I do not recall at any time authority being given to the benchers to take this type of action, so it it really a report which the minister should not have accepted.
Now we are asked to put the stamp of approval of the house on this report.
Nobody is asking that.
No.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the motion asks this house to examine a copy of this statement, which is the same thing.

All we want is to see
it; we do not want to approve it.

Perhaps the hon. member for Carleton will listen to me for a moment. We have now sanctified these benchers. The benchers are practising solicitors and lawyers and on occasion they appear before the bench. As the hon. gentleman for Greenwood pointed out, the bench is also composed of human beings with certain feelings. If one of the benchers appears before the judge, pleads a case and loses or is about to lose, will there not be some pressure on the judge to say to himself, "What is going to happen? This man is a bencher. He will go back to the benchers and they will find out that when I was 15, 16 or 14 I stole some apples". Who knows what the alleged crime might be? Will the judge

not take into consideration this motion and say, "The benchers may send another report to the minister and I will be"-
That is an insult to the whole judiciary of Canada.
Hear, hear.

It is not an insult. In dealing with this matter we should be not only pragmatic but truthful to ourselves and realize that we are providing the benchers with an aura they do not have. They are no different, as the hon. member for Greenwood pointed out, from any other individual. Surely a report or letter from any other organization, any common or average citizen or businessman would not be demanded by the house for tabling. That is the real issue, Mr. Speaker. Are we going to provide these benchers of the Upper Canada Law Society with some great sanctity and say they deserve it? That is what the motion calls for. I say we must consider this question very carefully. We might set a precedent and that would not be right; it would not help anyone. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I think the motion should be defeated.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate in this debate not for the purpose of adding any arithmetical weight to the opinions of the lawyers of the New Democratic party but rather to study with you the problems that are attendant on the tabling of these documents. I firmly believe that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) took the proper course in setting up a judicial inquiry and I commend him for that action. It was a very difficult problem to deal with and his actions were right in the circumstances. I feel that this problem is a judicial rather than a political one and it is very difficult to separate the two. If this document were tabled you would create a political climate which would greatly prejudice the fair trial of Mr. Justice Landreville.
It is not a trial; it is an inquiry.

I am sorry, Mr. Speaker; I mean that it would greatly prejudice the inquiry with regard to Mr. Justice Landreville. May I point out that the report prepared by the law society was one in which the justice played no part in the giving of any evidence, and I imagine that the rules of evidence applied to judicial cases were not closely followed. The report prepared by the benchers was merely an opinion of the
Motion for Papers
benchers with regard to the conduct of the particular judge. Therefore, to lay the report open at this time by tabling it would give particular members an opportunity to express opinions on a report which was obtained in a very limited way.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
My hon. friend from York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) is very disturbed that the highest court of the land is not going to deal with this problem. I would remind him that we will eventually deal with the problem after the report of the commissioner has been made. The hon. member also referred to the inquiry with regard to Atlantic Acceptance Corporation. I point out, Mr. Speaker, that was an inquiry with regard to a limited company whereas the inquiry that has been set up here is with regard to a particular person. I do not believe it has any particular application.
I respectfully submit to you, sir, that after listening to the speech of the hon. member for Carleton who moved this motion and the speeches of other members it is clear that the purpose of the motion seems to be political rather than judicial. I feel that no purpose would be served by creating a political climate prior to the inquiry.
The hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) thinks there is an aura of secrecy attached to this report. I respectfully submit there is no secrecy. At the moment there is a temporary delay and that delay is caused by the desire for a fair hearing. For these reasons I do not support the notice of motion but support the Minister of Justice.

Mr. Speaker, when I was listening to the presentation of this notice of motion by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) I found aspects which frankly troubled me when I attempted to follow his argument why this particular report should be produced. While waiting for my turn in this debate, I took the liberty of looking up Hansard for February 3 and reading again the words of the hon. member for Carleton when he presented his motion with his usual fire and eloquence. Let me draw the attention of the house to a few excerpts from his remarks. On page 669 of Hansard in the second column, he is reported as saying:
It is not the conduct of Mr. Justice Landreville with which this motion deals. Let me make that abundantly clear.

Motion for Papers
A few lines lower down on the page, I find this:
What I am interested in is the conduct of the Minister of Justice and of his predecessor, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau)-
On page 670, the third paragraph, he is reported as saying:
No, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that this motion is not designed in any way to relate to the hearing now abdicated by this parliament to a retired judge. It is designed-
I draw the attention of this house to these words:
___to get to immediate grips with the incompetence and inconsistency with which the Minister of Justice and his predecessor, the President of the Privy Council, have handled a vital matter affecting so delicately the whole principle of the independence of the judiciary-
At the conclusion of his remarks on page 670 I find this:
But I am determined to hold the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, who is now Minister of Justice, accountable for his conduct of the whole affair. For that reason I am asking hon. members in all parts of the house to support this motion, to strike a blow against the arrogance-I use that word deliberately-of the Minister of Justice-
In other words, he is not asking this house to approve the notice of motion to have this report put on the table of this house to permit parliament to decide on some action to protect against possible injury to the integrity of our judiciary; he is not asking this house to approve his notice of motion so that the house can be informed of some situation of which hon. members have had no knowledge at all. He is using this report to strike a political blow against the reputation of the Minister of Justice. In other words, in order to strike at the Minister of Justice he is willing to trample underfoot the rights of a Canadian citizen who happens to be a judge of one of our higher courts.
I suggest to hon. members that this is a very serious thing. Surely a judge as an individual has a right to be treated fairly. One of the great problems of our modern society is to what extent the rights of an individual have to be made subservient to the over-all rights of the state. We see this when we have debates on the rights of the press and the right of the individual to privacy, when we have discussions about the rights of the press to inform the public concerning judicial proceedings, even though this may be at the cost of a fair and impartial trial of the individual accused. I feel that this notice of motion by the hon. member for Carleton is an illustration of this problem of public policy

which we are facing in many avenues of our national life today.
Another aspect of this problem has been referred to in this house which I am not going to dead with here, namely, the very difficult problem involving a former civil servant and his rights which have come into conflict with a basic question of the over-all security of the state. This question has been referred to in the house during the question period and I would not be surprised if it is discussed again at some other time.
Returning to the subject matter of this motion, we have a situation in which the chief aim is a political attack leading to the embarrassment of the Minister of Justice. To do this, the hon. member for Carleton is willing to disregard completely, or so it appears to me, the ordinary civil rights of a Canadian citizen who in this case happens to be a judge of one of our superior courts.
This is simply ridiculous.

The hon. member says this is simply ridiculous. If that is the only criticism the hon. member can bring to bear on my argument, then my argument must have a lot more strength than he is willing to admit.
What are some of the basic things which someone who stands accused of a course of conduct, which if proven could lead to serious consequences, could expect as a matter of right as a Canadian citizen in our society today? Surely if the accusation is of the seriousness of that which is being brought by some at least in the public print against Mr. Justice Landreville, he has a right to expect that any report passing judgment on his conduct should be made after he has had a public hearing, after he has had a right to have counsel present arguments, after he has had the right to call witnesses and to have his counsel cross-examine witnesses. In short, there should be what might be called an adversary proceeding.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
If I may put it another way, he has the right to have the basic principles of British and Canadian justice followed. I recall Dean Smalley-Baker saying some years ago, when he was Dean of the Law School at Osgoode Hall, audi alterem partem, which I would gather means, "hear the other side." Surely this is a basic principle of British and Canadian justice which does not appear, so far as I am aware, to have been followed by those representatives of the Law Society who
February 17, 1966

prepared and submitted the report in question. I think that because this was not done this report in the form it has been presented to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) should not be presented to the house at this time.
If, Mr. Speaker, the question "How could this report be described or categorized" were put, the answer would be that it would be analogous to reports that are the result of preliminary investigations which are used for the purpose of deciding whether charges should be laid. I think those of my hon. friends who are perhaps more experienced and learned in the law than I happen to be at this time will agree that generally speaking such reports cannot be produced in courts where charges arising out of these preliminary investigations are brought.
One obvious reason for this is the one-sided nature of the preliminary report on which the decision to lay a charge has been based in the particular case. Often these reports contain what might be referred to as raw data, data which have not been completely checked out by the most detailed form of investigation, indeed, data which may not have been properly checked at all.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I think that those members of the house who have had more years experience at the bar than I have had will agree that it would be a very unfair and harmful thing if these confidential preliminary reports, on which investigations which lead to a decision to lay charges are often based, should be made available as documents of serious probitive consequence in the trial of the charges in question.
The question may be raised whether or not the person who has been charged with carrying out an inquiry into this judge's conduct will be deprived of some useful or valuable information because this report is not produced before this house at this time. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the Law Society will be able to be represented by counsel at the public hearing or at the private hearing, for that matter. It will be able through its counsel to make any sort of inquiry or argument it wishes. At the inquiry I am sure the Law Society will be able to request that witnesses be called to be heard by the person who will be conducting the inquiry if it appears that counsel for the inquiry will not be taking this step of his own accord. In fact, 1 would suspect that the Law Society will be able to present its report to the inquiry so that the judge can take such cognizance of it as would be relevant at the time.

If the report is presented to Mr. Justice Rand when he conducts his inquiry, it will be presented in a way which will open it to scrutiny by the representatives of Mr. Justice Landrevile. Inconsistencies or omissions in this report can be questioned and can be put on the public record.
If the motion that this report be now tabled is received and accepted by the house and if this report should be critical of the judge and his conduct, then I would suggest that this judgment in the report will become fixed in the public mind-it often appears that the public mind works this way-in a way which cannot be removed no matter what the decision of the inquiry held by Mr. Justice Rand. I suggest that members of the public will not be in a position to draw distinctions or raise criticisms of the type made so eloquently in this chamber today and on previous occasions by members from both sides of the house, pointing out the way this report has been prepared and presented.
For example, I am sure the public will not know that Mr. Justice Landreville was not heard before the report was produced; at least, that is the case as far as we are aware. They will not know that he did not have counsel appear for him before those who prepared the report and that there was not, even in the more limited sense of a public inquiry, a form of adversary proceeding in which his side was fully, fairly and effectively put before any decision was taken.
No, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that if this report is critical of the judge, and there seems to be some suspicion on the part of many that that may be the case, then there will be left in the public mind a form of taint on the reputation of the judge in question which no decision of Mr. Justice Rand's inquiry or even of this house may ever completely remove.
The result of this, I suggest, will be harmful not only to the reputation and general integrity of our judiciary itself; it will have done a form of irreparable harm to the reputation of Mr. Justice Landreville as an individual. It would be serious enough, Mr. Speaker, if the result of producing this report would be to harm unjustly in the public mind the reputation or integrity and high standards of our judieiary. It would be even worse if, to achieve a narrow, partisan, political purpose, the hon. member for Carleton were put in the position of harming a Canadian citizen who in this case may happen to be a judge of our Supreme Court.

Mr. Chairman, even if the minister is absent I should like to make some remarks which he might look up when he reads Hansard.
It is about the airport in Megantic. This airport was built by the Federal Government but it is not maintained. Owners of private planes who would like to use that airport, cannot do it in the fall or during the spring thaw. Even during winter the airport cannot be used.
I ask the minister whether he intends to set up a regional policy based on the needs of small airports?
The Megantic airport is modern enough, but the landing strips have not yet been paved.
I repeat this because the minister has just come into the house, privately owned planes cannot use it all year round.
In addition, when the summer is as wet as it was last year, even the provincial planes whose job is to protect the forests from fires often cannot land at this airport.
I know there is an agreement between the city and the federal government with regard to this airport; the city of Megantic rented the airport, but it cannot maintain it. I am quite convinced that at this particular time of the year planes cannot land there. The other day, private plane owners told us they

could neither take off nor land there because the runways were too deep in snow. In spring and in autumn, those landing strips are too soft, the ground is too soft to enable aircraft to take off or to land.
I would therefore ask the minister what he intends to do is such circumstances. Should the town of Megantic surrender the airport to the federal government, because it is unable to look after its maintenance. The citizens would like to be in a position to use it. The provincial government which also uses it for forest protection, would be interested in using it the year round.
I would ask the minister whether it would be possible to have in Megantic a profitable airport maintained by the federal government which would make sure that it is usable at all times.
Now I know of the representations the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) made regarding the Sherbrooke airport.
That airport is 45 miles from lake Megantic. It was built 4, 5 or 6 years ago, I think, and cost over $3 million, but it has never been used. The people of Megantic like those of the Sherbrooke area and of all the eastern townships would be anxious to use it.
I strongly support the hon. member for Sherbrooke in his request to have Air Canada establish an air route to serve Sherbrooke and the vicinity. That would be most helpful to us. The people of Lake Megantic and the eastern townships are in great need of this airport.
I would ask the minister to consider the situation. As this airport is already built, the only thing to do would be to authorize Air Canada to reinstate the services which this airport used to give. In my opinion, there would be enough passengers to make the line useful and profitable.
Those are the remarks I wanted to express to the minister; I ask him to take into consideration the matter of Megantic and Sherbrooke airports.

Mr. Chairman, it is almost two years since the White Paper on Defence was tabled in this house. During those two years, the Department of National Defence has been busily engaged in implementing the policies set out in the White Paper, including sweeping changes in its organization forecast at that time.
In introducing the 1964-65 estimates, I summarized my remarks by stating:
-that notwithstanding the reduction in expenditures, we will have achieved, within two years, a significant qualitative improvement and operational capability of our armed forces.
That improvement is being achieved as I shall outline for you in the course of my remarks today.
First, I should like to take this opportunity, on behalf of my associate and myself, to pay tribute to all those in the department whose diligent work has contributed so much to the success of this immense project. As hon. members are aware, each new step has to be carefully studied and evaluated in relation to the whole and in relation to the final objective. The fact that our progress towards a completely unified functional force is well in advance of what we might reasonably have hoped for reflects the spirit and enthusiasm with which the task has been undertaken.
I should like also to publicly thank my Associate Minister for his wonderful co-operation. He carries the bulk of the administrative load in the department and performs his tasks in a most efficient manner. Without his help it would be impossible to cope with the extraordinarily heavy work load in the department, particularly during this period of intense activity.
As hon. members are well aware, the probability of a major war arising directly between the NATO powers on the one hand and the Soviet Union and the Warsaw pact powers on the other is remote and would be disastrous for east and west alike. Nevertheless we must recognize that the political
February 17, 1966

problems of central Europe are not yet resolved and the Soviet military capability is not only being maintained but steadily enhanced. We continue to regard our membership in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and our military support to it as being important to our security.
It is clear that instability in other parts of the world has, and will continue to result in conflicts which can endanger our security. Canada has been able to contribute military forces in some of these potentially dangerous situations to provide the stability for the political actions necessary for a peaceful solution to proceed unfettered by the bitterness and passions of active hostilities. No one, I believe, can be certain that circumstances will not arise in the future where active participation of Canadian forces would be in the interests of our national security. The military forces of today must have the capability of responding quickly, and the flexibility to meet a wide variety of demands that may be placed upon them to protect the security of this country. This, among other things, means first class personnel, appropriate equipment to provide the required flexibility, means of rapid transport and an organizational structure from the headquarters down which can provide clear and decisive direction. There is still much to be done to achieve the military posture that we have set out to achieve, but I am satisfied that we are well along the road and I propose to give you some of the facts that substantiate this conclusion.
In order that Canada's armed forces might make the maximum contribution in terms of effectiveness to the deterrents of war and the maintenance of peace, it was announced in the White Paper in March, 1964, that the headquarters of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force would be integrated on a functional basis as a first step toward a single unified defence force for Canada. This functional integration began on August 1, 1964 and has been going forward continuously since that date. Integration of the staffs at Canadian forces headquarters is now largely complete. Already the total number of persons employed at headquarters has been reduced by more that 1,000 and the work is continuing as efficiently and, in the opinion of the most senior departmental officers, more effectively than ever before. When the one time work load due to the changes related to the integration process itself have been performed, a

Supply-National Defence total reduction in staff of approximately 30 per cent will have been achieved.
The second step in the integration process was the development of a new command structure for the Canadian armed forces. This structure had to be efficient in design, consistent in pattern, require a minimum of overhead, and responsive and effective from a military point of view. On June 7, 1965, fully three months ahead of schedule, a new functional command structure, in which the former eleven commands were reduced to six, was announced. These were, mobile command, maritime command, air defence command, air transport command, materiel command and training command. The No. 1 air division in Europe and the No. 4 Canadian Infantry Brigade group in Europe were left to continue to report directly to the Chief of the Defence Staff in order to maintain maximum operational effectiveness during the transitional period. Now, six months later, all the command headquarters have been created and either have assumed or are in the process of assuming their new responsibilities.
The formation of mobile command is basic to the philosophy of Canada's new defence policy. The largest of the new functional commands, its task is to operationally train and maintain the land elements of the Canadian force and its tactical air support, and to keep this force in a state of combat readiness which will enable it to be deployed in units of the required size to meet Canadian commitments and undertakings anywhere in the world. These commitments range from reinforcing the European sector as a contribution to the deterrence of general war, to United Nations peace keeping operations. The prime ingredients in the force are quick reaction-time, the ability to go where required with dispatch, and to perform its tasks with maximum effectiveness. The decision to introduce into this command, which was formed officially October 19, 1965, tactical air squadrons equipped with the new CF-5 will increase to a marked extent both the capability and flexibility of the mobile force. Tactics and doctrines will be developed as the squadrons are formed and are able to exercise with the land elements they are required to support.
The acquisition of the Voyageur helicopter and the de Havilland Buffalo, short take-off and landing military transport will give the mobile command a greatly enhanced tactical capability. Strategic transport for mobile command will be provided by air transport

Supply-National Defence command, and the sea element by maritime command.
The special service force concept, announced in the White Paper to apply to one brigade, has now been expanded and current plans call for two brigades to be converted, on a planned basis, to this concept of air transportability, with an additional airborne battalion group for added flexibility and quick response to domestic needs and overseas commitments as they arise.
The primary mission of maritime command continues to be the anti-submarine role. Its secondary role, as stated in the White Paper, is the provision of sealift and other related naval capability to mobile command. Maritime command was officially formed on January 19, 1966, and the integration of the naval and air elements under one commander will provide an even closer relationship between the various units engaged in the same basic mission. Headquarters, maritime command, is at Halifax, while the deputy commander, maritime commander Pacific, will have his headquarters at Esquimalt, British Columbia.

The fleet modernization program announced last year is continuing. The post second world war destroyer escorts, refitted with modern equipment, have an antisubmarine surveillance and operational capability far greater than ever before. The introduction of helicopters as part of the weapons system has contributed markedly to this increased capability from the standpoint of range, speed, area of coverage, and general effectiveness. The introduction of ASROC, a long-range, rocket-assisted torpedo delivery system, will provide an additional substantial increase in target-destruction capability.
The most recent addition to maritime command has been H.M.C.S. Ojibwa, the first of three "O" class submarines. These submarines have the dual capability of providing the rest of the antisubmarine forces with antisubmarine warfare training and at the same time being additional operational units. In April, the First Canadian Submarine Squadron will be formed to operate out of Halifax. The Argus, Neptune and Tracker aircraft assigned to maritime command are also receiving mid-life re-equipment which will provide them with an improved capability.
Materiel Command, with headquarters at Rockcliffe, is being organized to provide logistic support of the Canadian armed forces. It

will be charged with the responsibility of providing faster, more efficient service and at the same time of eliminating the duplication and triplication which exists with three separate supply systems. By making full use of electronic data processing equipment, it will eventually be possible to provide better service, maintain smaller inventories and at the same time to operate with substantially fewer personnel, thus freeing more of the armed forces establishment for operational requirements.
Training command, with headquarters in Winnipeg, will provide the individual training, including flying training and trades training, for all service personnel required by the Canadian armed forces. The introduction of the M.113 armoured personnel carrier to our NATO brigade group in Europe is now nearly complete. This has given the brigade group a greatly enhanced operational capability and, for the first time, the armoured protection it would need in the face of a fully mechanized opponent. The delivery of the ENT AC and SS.ll anti-tank guided missiles will be augmented by the introduction of the Carl Gustav medium antitank weapon now coming into service. I would like to say a word here about the expertise of our airmen who are serving with the air division in Europe. This professionalism has been evident from the very first days of our air division in Europe; first flying Sabre jets and then the CF-lOO's, our fliers consistently won the Guynmeyer trophy which is emblematic of air combat supremacy.

The capability of the ground environment for air defence against the manned bomber is being enhanced despite the fact that a decreasing amount of our resources are going into this area. This is being done by the introduction of a back-up system which will provide the continuous air surveillance and control of air defence weapons. In December, Canada was asked to provide air units for the Zambian oil airlift. On December 22, an advanced party left Canada, and on the 30th the first oil airlift was effectively carried out. The response to this request and the quick reaction capability clearly demonstrated the effectiveness of the Canadian armed forces to meet contingencies.
The ground forces too are continually exercising their quick-reaction capability. The 1st Battalion Black Watch battalion group, currently designated as Canada's contribution to the Allied Command Europe mobile force, has recently undergone a strenuous training program, designated Exercise White Caribou, in Newfoundland. On February 27 this battalion group will participate in Exercise Winter Express, scheduled for northern Norway. This will provide an opportunity to practise its role along with the five other NATO nations participating. It will be the first time that the Canadian armed forces have attempted to airlift a battalion group over a considerable distance in a realistic time frame. This exercise, therefore, plays a most important part in the continued development of the strategic mobile force concept.
It may interest hon. members to know that 18 or 19 Air Transport Command heavy aircraft will be employed in this airlift, and that in addition HMCS Provider, our operational support ship on the east coast, will participate in the deployment and re-deployment phases of the exercise.

One of the most important developments in respect to the reserve forces has been the appointment to Canadian Forces Headquarters of Major-General W. A. B. Anderson as Deputy Chief, Reserves. General Anderson will, in fact, be the commander of the reserve forces in Canada and have the responsibility for their organization and training in support of the regular forces as well as in aid of the civil power, and their supplementary role in national survival. The Deputy Chief, Reserves, heads a sub-branch at headquarters which is being organized on an integrated basis and which will have full responsibility for the reserve components and cadets of the navy, army and air force.
The first task to be undertaken by this section is the re-organization of its field command structure for reserve units following the termination of the existing army regional and district commands. The appointment of an officer of the rank of major-general underlines the continued importance of the reserve forces in support of the regular forces.
With the re-organization of the Canadian Army Militia last year and the re-introduction of corps training, a new vigour and effectiveness is developing. It is intended to increase the momentum by improved training opportunities in the coming year. Where possible, militia units will be given an opportunity to visit regular units at home stations for the purpose of obtaining instruction and practice in using the latest items of operational equipment. Recently militiamen of several eastern Canadian armoured regiments were flown into Camp Gagetown where the Royal Canadian Dragoons conducted a program of week end training for them. The experiment was extremely successful and will be used as a pattern for similar exercises of this nature in the future.
The reserves in their new posture are being counted upon to make an important contribution to Canada's security. The volunteers to whom this task has been entrusted are worthy of our highest respect and admiration.
I would like now to discuss briefly some of the changes in management techniques which have been introduced into the department since 1963 in conjunction with the reorganization.
Two of the most important problems in defence management were the reconciliation of the programs of the three services, that is, the setting of the real priorities between the programs of each and gauging the effects of
February 17, 1966

each program not just in terms of capital cost, but also in terms of support requirements, personnel and annual recurring costs.
The integration of navy, army and air force headquarters aided materially in the solution of the first of these problems. An integrated defence program has been established. This displays all approved National Defence activities and forecasts spending over the current year and the following five-year period. The program data relates the various military functions and missions to resource requirements of manpower, money and materiel. With this information available, it is possible to determine at once the implications both on a particular mission and on the integrated defence program as a whole, of any new requirement.
The defence programming system includes a program change procedure which keeps the IDP current as it reflects changing national and international conditions and the adoption of advantageous technological advances.
The development of this comprehensive system has been taking place for some months. To assist in its implementation, we have retained a consultant group familiar with the process, to advise us. Our present integrated defence plan should be programmed and the system in full operation in 1966. This will enormously simplify the preparation of the estimates for 1967-68. The operation of this system insists on the solution of the two management problems raised: First, as it includes all missions and the elements of all missions, it displays each of these in a way which facilitates the consideration of priorities and demands their solution. Second, the data required for the system includes capital costs, personnel and support requirements, and operating costs, and therefore the total effect of each new program change is known at the outset and available for review at any time. Thus all of the information necessary for management to make decisions is readily available and the system itself ensures that the data is presented in a manner that leads to realistic decisions.

Another improvement in management techniques has been the granting of authority to use the proceeds of the sale of surplus equipment by the department for the purchase of new equipment. This year, on an experimental basis, this system has also been applied to real properties up to the limit of $5 million. This policy was suggested by the Royal
Supply-National Defence Commission on Government Organization. The reasoning behind it is obvious. It provides an incentive to management to make decisions. If there is no advantage in selling surplus materials and properties, there is a natural tendency to postpone serious consideration. When the proceeds are available for new high priority projects, however, there is a strong motivation to take a hard look at inventories and to make realistic decisions. In the fiscal year 1964-65 approximately $7 million revenue was obtained from the sale of surplus materials, supplies and equipment, and $4,744,000 has been realized from this source for 1965-66 to the end of December. During the current fiscal year as of December 31, real estate sales have totalled $1,589,000. These sales reduce the cost of maintenance of the inventories.
Another important area which has been subject to re-organization is that of development. Each service had its own development vote, and in each case the administration and screening was carried out by the Defence Research Board, following receipt of submissions from the services. The system tended to be inflexible and slow. Program changes had to go through the whole system and the amount of time consumed was so great that the project momentum was often lost and the initial Canadian advantage overtaken by development projects in other countries.
The classic case is the armoured personnel carrier, the Bobcat-V.C. This project was out front at the outset but, due to the rigidities of the system and the decision-making process, all the initial advantage was lost and the project overtaken by developments elsewhere.
The simulator is another recent example.

In order to develop a more flexible system, a number of important changes have been put into effect. The service development votes have been built into a single development vote in consonance with integration. Administration of development projects has been given to the services themselves. The Defence Research Board input and screening now takes place during the initial stage of the project definition in order to determine at that stage if the proposal is scientifically feasible.
A management group has been formed called the development and associated research policy group under the chairmanship of the chief of technical services. This group

The increased emphasis on research and development is in fulfilment of the policy laid down in the White Paper that there would be a modest but consistent increase in these activities. The Defence Research Board has the responsibility not only of providing scientific advice to the minister and to the chief of defence staff, but also of undertaking pure and applied research on behalf of the defence forces. Canada continues to enjoy a well-deserved reputation for extraordinary results in research, particularly in relation to the resources made available for that purpose.
One of the Defence Research Board's most dramatic achievements in 1965 was in the space research field. The successful launch of Alouette II in November in an elliptical orbit was the climax of months and years of painstaking research and development. As of late January it had completed 720 orbits about the earth, travelling 22,800,000 miles, and had executed 8,175 commands while operating six hours a day to produce 54,000 ionagrams.
Isis "A", the board's third satellite, is scheduled for launch next year. It will carry ten experiments and is scheduled to move in an elliptical orbit some 300 to 2,600 statute miles above the earth. As the sun's period of activity increases with more frequent and violent solar storms, this space craft should provide most useful data.

The Defence Research Board's industrial research assistance program introduced late in 1961, to encourage industry in Canada to establish additional research facilities, has proven to be a most successful activity. As I stated at the outset, the strength of the Canadian armed forces is in the dedication, training and professionalism of its officers and men. Just as no force, no matter how well trained, can operate effectively without good equipment, similarly no amount of modern equipment, by itself, can be effective without persons skilled and trained in its use.
We have in the past enjoyed, and still enjoy, a tremendously proud and effective force, unsurpassed anywhere in the world. We fully recognize that if we are to maintain this effectiveness in the future, we must continue to provide the training, remuneration and career opportunities to attract the high calibre of person required for our demanding tasks.
Whereas it is true that re-organization of any kind raises questions in respect to the effects that it may have on individuals, the important problems relating to individuals in the armed forces today are not those resulting from integration, they are the same real problems affecting men and women in all walks of life, that is, pay, allowances, housing, career opportunities, etc. I might add that perhaps there are many Canadians who do not fully appreciate just how good the

The

actual evidence in regard to recruiting, loss of men from the services, the situation in regard to the effectiveness of units, and the ability to keep units operating, all points in this direction. I shall be outlining a considerable number of these things in the course of my remarks.
I would like to put more emphasis on this matter of morale. Everyone with any military experience, particularly with experience in war, knows that the most important single requirement for efficient and effective individual fighting men, units and formations, is high morale. Without it you cannot have efficiency and effectiveness in any military organization.
An article which bears on this, and which appeared in the Victoria Colonist of January 26, is something I would like to put on the record at this time. It is headed "Confidence" and reads:
In a recent address to the directors of Victoria's Armed Service Centre one of Canada s outstanding seamen, Rear Admiral J. C. Hibbard, discussed the meaning of morale in a military organization.
To the individual serviceman-regardless of his ranks-morale is the result of a combination of many factors, the admiral said.

By outlining this simple definition at a time when our national defence policies present such a confused picture both at home and to the outside world, Admiral Hibbard might have done a great service to Canada.

This decline in morale is forcefully illustrated by the large number of personnel who have left the armed services of their own volition. I do not refer to those who were dismissed or put out for disciplinary reasons, I refer to only those who have left of their own volition. These people could not see any future in the armed forces because they have no motivation to remain. This is illustrated by a return to a question by the hon. member for Edmonton West to be found at page 781 of Hansard for February 7. The return was made in answer to question No. 4 which asked for the number of persons who were retired from the defence forces at their own request prior to normal retirement age. The answer was 13,142. Nothing like this has ever taken place in the history of the Canadian armed forces and it indicates exactly what I have just said, that a very large proportion of those people in the armed forces have lost their morale and want to get out because they feel they have no future and are not doing a necessary job.
This same return indicates that a high proportion of these 13,000 odd individuals who left at their own request were highly trained officers, N.C.O.'s and specialists who are essential to the efficient operation of any modern military force.
In answer to a question I asked, to be found in Hansard for February 9 another return was made which shows what the reduction in the strength of the armed forces has been. We find that it dropped from approximately 124,000 in 1961-62 to approximately 109,000 at the end of December, 1965. At the present time, according to press reports, the strength is now below 107,000. During that same period this report indicates that enlistments had dropped from 16,526 in 1961 to 10,415 in 1965. Last year the losses of the armed forces personnel totalled 17,696, all ranks, which is a total loss or wastage of 7,281, or a rate of wastage of some 600 men per month.
These figures show two things. First of all, they show that it has become increasingly difficult to get people to enlist in the services and second, a very large proportion of highly trained personnel are getting out. In addition to the ones who have got out there are quite a number who are trying to get out but who 23033-9U
Supply-National Defence have not been released. I have referred several of these cases to the minister and the associate minister, but I do not know how many there are. The number must be considerable today. These people would get out if they could but the department, because of the shortage of trained personnel at this time, will not allow them to do so.
The loss of so many highly trained personnel is very serious and has caused a decline in the quality and effectiveness of our defence forces. This is manifested by the situation which exists now in all three of the defence forces. Let us take the navy as a first example to see what has happened there.
When the minister was sworn in the navy had 43 anti-submarine vessels in commission and in operation including, of course, the Bonaventure, destroyer escorts and frigates. In addition we had two flotillas of mine sweepers. What ships does the navy now have? As close as I can determine we now have 34 antisubmarine vessels and no mine sweepers. Of the 34 antisubmarine vessels we have left there are five or six laid up at Halifax and two at Esquimalt because of a lack of sufficiently trained personnel to man them. This means there are seven or eight vessels which cannot go to sea. We now have some 27 operational fighting ships left in our navy. That is far below the number that we are committed to provide as part of our contribution to the NATO affiance, and far below the number required for the many other responsibilities the navy would have in the event of war. In spite of this, the minister keeps on saying and has been saying for the last two years, that the effectiveness of the armed forces has improved.
That is true.

The minister suggests that is true, but I ask any reasonable person in this chamber how it could be true when the number of fighting ships has decreased seriously, with a large percentage of the ones left not able to go to sea because of the lack of trained personnel to man them.
Because they are old ships, now obsolete.

The minister suggests that the ships we now have are much more efficient and up to date than the ones we had, but that is not the case. With one or two exceptions we have the same ships. I believe one or two have been put into service in the last two or three years with slightly improved

In view of all these facts it is nonsense to say that the effectiveness of the navy is anything like it was before the minister was sworn in. I do not think there is a naval man in this country or anywhere in the world who would not agree with that statement.

IMMIGRATION-REPORTED INCREASE IN APPLICATIONS FROM RUMANIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I raised a question on Tuesday afternoon that I felt was of some concern. I have received representations on this matter since the election and 1 know that the question of the situation in eastern Europe has been eloquently dealt with in this house by a previous speaker. This matter was brought to my mind by an article which appeared in a magazine called The Tablet entitled "Hungarians in Transylvania." This article was written by Judith Listowel and appeared in the January 8 edition of this magazine. It was the second of two articles. Dealing with the situation of this minority group in Rumania the article contains the following passage:
"Now there are rumours of a mass emigration to Canada. Thousands of Hungarian peasants have put their names down, for they do not see any future for their children here. I do not know whether they will actually receive their emigration passports, or whether this is just a hoax, but I rather think that they might, for if they go their places can be taken by more and more settlers from Old Rumania, and gradually the Hungarian character of Transylvania will be wiped out."
It was this article that prompted my question to the minister in charge of immigration and I asked whether there had been an unusual number of applications received this year from potential emigrants from that country. I should like to ask a further question, whether the ministry has been at all aware of the situation suggested in this article, namely that people in a foreign country

may be the victims of a very elaborate hoax with regard to the possibility of their emigrating to Canada.
